headline_findings: This comparison covers two papers - one on Lyme disease and one on Long COVID - and does not describe either condition in general.

The Lyme disease paper contains extensive diagnostic-delay, access-barrier, and healthcare-utilization figures that the Long COVID paper does not address at all, while the Long COVID paper contains income- and education-stratified financial-hardship probabilities that the Lyme disease paper does not report.

Neither paper supplies a direct patient out-of-pocket dollar figure: the Lyme disease paper cites one external, claims-based $1,000,000,000/year estimate, and the Long COVID paper reports only percentage-point changes in the probability of a hardship event, with no dollar amounts at all.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper cites an external, claims-based estimate of $1,000,000,000/year in U.S. healthcare costs tied to retreatment of diagnosed Lyme patients, but this is not the paper's own patient-level out-of-pocket figure and no price year is given.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports no dollar-denominated cost figure of any kind; all of its burden measures are percentage-point changes in the probability of a hardship event (food insecurity, inability to pay bills, threatened loss of utility service), not expenditures.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: A reader comparing the two conditions' cost burden would find one externally cited aggregate dollar figure for Lyme disease and no dollar figure at all for Long COVID in these two papers.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 77% of persistent Lyme disease patients were not diagnosed until the late or chronic stage (over 6 months), a 32-percentage-point gap in prior misdiagnosis between persistent and acute patients, and that 86% of surveyed clinicians cite inadequate physician education as a reason for delayed diagnosis.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not tag or report any diagnostic-delay figures.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Diagnostic delay is a central, heavily documented theme in the Lyme disease paper and is entirely absent from the Long COVID paper in this comparison.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that, among persistent Lyme disease patients with a work-schedule impact, 62% reduced work hours and 30% quit work altogether, and that 35% of persistent Lyme disease patients report disability as their employment status.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper finds that lost or reduced work hours account for a 0.65 percentage-point portion of the bill-payment-hardship increase among income groups, and more broadly that 6%-20% of the long-COVID-to-financial-hardship association is mediated by lost employment or reduced work hours.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers separately identify work or income disruption as a contributing channel of economic burden, even though they measure it with different metrics (employment-status percentages versus a mediated share of a hardship probability).

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 50% of persistent Lyme disease patients' physicians do not accept insurance, and that roughly 75% of surveyed Lyme-treating clinicians do not participate in insurance networks.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not tag or report an access-barriers category; it measures financial hardship events rather than provider-access or insurance-acceptance barriers.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Provider-level access barriers are documented only in the Lyme disease paper among these two papers.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports a ratio of 17.8 for persistent Lyme disease patients' annual doctor visits compared to the general-population comparator, and separately states 19.4 annual doctor visits versus 1.09 for the general population, and 3.7 annual ER visits versus 0.43.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not report healthcare utilization counts such as doctor or ER visits; it measures only the probability of financial-hardship events.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Readers looking for visit-count or utilization-intensity evidence will find it only in the Lyme disease paper among these two papers.

comparison_rows.dimension: How cited or modeled figures may undercount the burden

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper notes that its cited $1,000,000,000/year estimate is drawn from insurance-claims records, and by the paper's own account roughly 50% of persistent Lyme disease patients' physicians do not accept insurance, so this estimate may produce lower or different counts in the setting studied.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not include an undercounting-related limitation in its caveats, and it does not report any cost estimate that could be checked against an alternative data source.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Lyme disease paper flags a specific mechanism (claims-based data excluding non-insurance-accepting providers) by which its cited cost figure may produce lower or different counts in the setting studied.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper presents its $1,000,000,000/year cost estimate and its 2,000,000-person cumulative persistent-Lyme-disease estimate as single national pooled figures with no breakdown by age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or similar subgroups.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper disaggregates its hardship-probability estimates only by income and education level, with no further breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or similar subgroups despite these being used as regression covariates.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers separately report figures that are pooled or only partly stratified, limiting how precisely either paper's burden estimates can be applied to specific demographic groups.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper states it has no direct patient out-of-pocket spending or total dollar cost figures from its own registry, and no lifetime or multi-year cost projection.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper states its data 'do not allow' exploration of the healthcare-cost pathway to financial hardship, and it has no symptom-severity or duration-beyond-3-months data to link to a cost or hardship gradient.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers separately acknowledge that a direct medical-cost or spending pathway remains unmeasured in their own data.

shared_themes.theme: Neither paper provides a patient-level, condition-specific dollar figure for out-of-pocket spending; where a dollar figure exists at all (Lyme disease), it comes from an external claims-based source rather than the paper's own registry data, and the Long COVID paper has no dollar figure whatsoever.

evidence.note: The paper's own registry reports utilization counts (e.g., 19.4 annual doctor visits) without attached unit costs, and relies on an externally cited Adrion et al. 2015 claims-based $1,000,000,000/year figure.
The paper explicitly states its data 'do not allow' exploration of the healthcare-cost pathway, and all its burden measures are percentage-point hardship probabilities, not dollar amounts.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers separately identify lost or reduced work/employment as a contributing channel to overall burden, even though they quantify it with different metrics.

evidence.note: 62% of persistent Lyme disease patients with a work-schedule impact reduced hours and 30% quit work altogether, and 35% report disability as their employment status.
Lost or reduced work hours account for 6%-20% of the long-COVID-to-financial-hardship association across subgroups.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers report figures that are only partly disaggregated, limiting breakdown by demographic subgroups beyond their primary stratifiers.

evidence.note: The $1,000,000,000/year cost estimate and 2,000,000-person cumulative estimate are pooled national figures with no breakdown by age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or similar subgroups.

Hardship-probability estimates are disaggregated only by income and education, not by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or similar subgroups despite these being included as regression covariates.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper documents extensive diagnostic delay and misdiagnosis, including a 57-percentage-point gap in persistent-disease rates between late- and early-diagnosed patients and a 32-percentage-point misdiagnosis gap between persistent and acute patients.

evidence.note: 77% of persistent Lyme disease patients were not diagnosed until the late/chronic stage, and 86% of surveyed clinicians cite inadequate physician education as a reason for delay.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper documents provider-level access barriers, including insurance non-acceptance by about half of patients' physicians.

evidence.note: 50% of persistent Lyme disease patients report their physician does not accept insurance, and roughly 75% of surveyed clinicians do not participate in insurance networks.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper describes a systemic gap between a growing patient population and the research and clinical infrastructure available to treat them.

evidence.note: The paper states 'very little research has been conducted' on treating persistent Lyme disease, and only 4% of persistent Lyme disease patients are seen by infectious disease specialists.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper measures financial hardship as the probability of specific hardship events (food insecurity, inability to pay bills, threatened utility shutoff), stratified by income and education, rather than as a dollar cost or diagnostic-access measure.

evidence.note: Long COVID was linked to a higher probability of all three hardship measures across nearly all income and education groups, with the effect generally strongest for the lowest-income households.

evidence_gaps_shared: Neither paper provides a direct, patient-level, condition-specific dollar figure for out-of-pocket medical spending tied to its own underlying data source.

Neither paper's reported figures are broken down by race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status, even where some of these variables appear elsewhere in the underlying data (e.g., as regression covariates in the Long COVID paper).
cross_analysis.summary: This comparison covers two papers - the Lyme disease paper (one persistent Lyme disease patient-registry chartbook) and the Long COVID paper (one BRFSS-based financial-hardship study) - and does not describe either condition in general. The Lyme disease paper is rich in diagnostic-delay, access-barrier, and healthcare-utilization detail but offers only one externally cited aggregate dollar figure rather than its own patient-level cost data. The Long COVID paper is rich in income- and education-stratified financial-hardship probabilities, with employment loss identified as a partial contributing channel, but contains no dollar costs, diagnostic-delay data, or access-barrier data at all. Where the two papers overlap, it is on the general idea that work/employment disruption contributes to burden and that both papers' figures are only partly disaggregated by demographic subgroup; elsewhere, the two papers largely cover different dimensions of burden rather than the same dimension measured differently.
cross_analysis.limitations: This analysis rests on a small, non-random sample: as given in the real_stats, there is 1 paper in the Lyme disease group and 1 paper in the Long COVID group, with 0 papers in the cross or other groups, so this is not a controlled study and cannot be generalized beyond these two specific papers and the documents each was built from.

learning_cards.headline: Half of persistent Lyme patients report insurance not accepted
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper reports that 50 percent of persistent Lyme disease patients say their physician does not accept insurance.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper's results are not tagged to a burden category here; its findings appear elsewhere on the page.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers measure what share of patients encounter providers who do not accept insurance, to see whether a similar access barrier shows up?

learning_cards.headline: Persistent Lyme patients report much more pre-diagnosis misdiagnosis
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper finds a 32 percentage point gap in misdiagnosis rates between persistent and acute Lyme disease patients.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper's results are not tagged to a burden category here; its findings appear elsewhere on the page.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID studies compare misdiagnosis rates between patients with shorter versus longer-lasting symptoms, the way the Lyme disease paper compares persistent and acute groups?

learning_cards.headline: One cited estimate puts yearly Lyme retreatment cost at a billion dollars
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper cites an external, claims-based estimate of 1000000000 USD/year in U.S. healthcare costs tied to Lyme disease retreatment, rather than presenting its own patient-level cost data.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper's results are not tagged to a burden category here; its findings appear elsewhere on the page.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could a comparable claims-based aggregate cost estimate be built for ongoing or repeated Long COVID care?

learning.takeaway: The Long COVID paper could ask whether insurance-access barriers, misdiagnosis gaps, and aggregate retreatment costs like those the Lyme disease paper reports also apply to Long COVID, while the Lyme disease paper could ask whether BRFSS-style financial-hardship measures could be developed for Lyme disease, since the Long COVID paper's own findings here are not tagged to a burden category and appear elsewhere on the page.
